FUNDING: Gates Foundation.

title: When time is not the same: pre-hospital delay and perforation in global appendicitis care
abstract: Acute appendicitis sits at the centre of one of surgery's oldest debates: does perforation occur because treatment is delayed or because some patients are biologically predisposed to perforation regardless of timing? The prospective global cohort study by Theophilus TK Anyomih and colleagues, published in The Lancet Global Health, provides some of the strongest evidence to date that pre-hospital delay matters.1 Among 45 218 patients treated in 1372 hospitals across 112 countries, longer pre-hospital time was associated with a clear dose-response increase in perforation risk, reaching an adjusted risk ratio of 1·61 (95% CI 1·44–1·80) for delays of 72 h or longer compared with delays of less than 12 h.

title: Mid-upper arm circumference of preschool-aged children during conflict transition in the Gaza Strip: a cross-sectional nutritional surveillance study
abstract: BACKGROUND: In August, 2025, preschool children in Gaza faced excessive wasting, including famine conditions in Gaza City. Following a declared ceasefire in October, 2025, supplies entering Gaza increased. However, trends in preschool child nutritional status have not been reported in peer-reviewed journals. Therefore, we aimed to assess the prevalence of wasting among children in the Gaza Strip following a declared ceasefire. METHODS: In this cross-sectional nutritional surveillance study conducted by the UN Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East, children aged 6-59 months visiting ten health centres and 27 medical points within school shelters and tented camps across the Gaza Strip for food supplements, feeding programme eligibility, vaccines, and treatments, were screened by mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) measurement. Children with MUAC measurements of less than 125 mm were referred for therapeutic feeding. Age-sex-specific MUAC Z scores derived from WHO reference curves were evaluated to estimate semi-monthly prevalence of wasting (ie, a MUAC Z score of <-2) and severe wasting (ie, a MUAC Z score of <-3), overall and stratified by age (ie, 6-11, 12-23, and 24-59 months), sex, type of facility, and governorate. Data were collected and entered by trained staff at the time of visits directly onto a standardised Microsoft Excel template designed for MUAC screening. Trends in wasting were compared with extant online reports of the Gaza Chamber of Commerce & Industry on numbers of trucks entering Gaza (70-97% carrying food) and the World Food Programme Palestine monthly report on market prices of brown lentils, a local staple, as indicators of food availability and access. The primary outcomes were to admit malnourished children aged 6-59 months into Community Management of Acute Malnutrition programmes based on MUAC measurements and to estimate trends in the prevalence of wasting malnutrition among these children. FINDINGS: From Aug 1, 2025, to April 30, 2026, 78 902 unique children were screened with 101 456 MUAC measurements, including 75 687 (95·8%) children in the Khan Younis, Middle, and Gaza City Governorates. Children were evenly distributed by sex, with 39 362 (49·9%) females and 39 540 (50·1%) males. 17 158 (21·7%) children were aged 6-11 months, 20 552 (26·0%) were aged 12-23 months, and 41 192 (52·2%) children were aged 24-59 months. The prevalence of wasting declined from 15·7% (1235/7857; 95% CI 14·9-16·5) in mid-August, 2025, to 3·2% (180/5714; 2·7-3·7) by late April, 2026, including in Khan Younis from 12·8% (357/2793; 11·6-14·1) to 2·8% (58/2104; 2·1-3·5), Middle from 8·5% (242/2838; 7·5-9·6) to 3·0% (44/1451; 2·2-4·0), and Gaza City from 28·6% (636/2226; 26·7-30·5) to 4·0% (70/1738; 3·2-5·1). Wasting was more prevalent in males and initially higher in younger children but decreased to 5% or less in all groups. Wasting generally tracked trends in truck entry and lentil market prices. INTERPRETATION: Preschool child wasting declined in Gaza over 9 months from active war to 6 months post-ceasefire, despite continued military attacks and severely constrained living conditions. Comprehensive nutritional monitoring and sustained dietary adequacy are essential to protect children's health in Gaza. FUNDING: UN Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East.

title: Pre-hospital time and risk of perforation in patients with acute appendicitis in 112 countries (AlliGatOr): an international, prospective, observational cohort study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Acute appendicitis is the most common surgical emergency worldwide. Concern that delayed treatment might increase perforation can lead to unnecessary surgery and high rates of negative appendicectomy, where a normal, non-inflamed appendix is removed. However, whether perforation is related to pre-hospital time (symptom onset to first surgical assessment) has not been explored in contemporary global data. METHODS: We conducted an international, multicentre, prospective, observational cohort study (AlliGatOr) of patients undergoing emergency appendicectomy for suspected acute appendicitis in 1377 hospitals across 112 countries. We included all consecutive eligible patients and excluded patients undergoing appendicectomy for indications other than suspected acute appendicitis. Each participating hospital entered data from medical records prospectively into the Research Electronic Data Capture platform. The primary outcome was perforation and the primary exposure was pre-hospital time (categorised as <12 h, 12-23 h, 24-47 h, 48-71 h, and ≥72 h). Follow-up was for 30 days after surgery to assess postoperative outcomes. In-hospital time (first surgical assessment to skin incision) was a key secondary exposure. We estimated adjusted risk ratios (aRRs) using multilevel Poisson regression. Multivariable analyses used complete cases; missing data were not imputed. The study is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06774001) and is completed. FINDINGS: Between Feb 3 and May 25, 2025, we enrolled 45 218 patients with a median age of 27 years (IQR 18-41); 25 218 (55·8%) were male and 19 996 (44·2%) were female. 42 317 patients were included in the primary analysis, of whom 13 560 (32·0%) had perforation. The adjusted primary model included 41 740 patients with complete covariate data. Access to CT imaging varied across income groups: 12 232 (58·6%) of 20 861 patients in high-income countries, 4597 (37·1%) of 12 388 in upper-middle-income countries, 1769 (19·2%) of 9192 in lower-middle-income countries, and 156 (5·6%) of 2769 in low-income countries. Minimally invasive surgery was used in 19 985 (95·8%) of 20 861 patients, 6817 (55·0%) of 12 390, 2613 (28·4%) of 9195, and 203 (7·3%) of 2770, respectively. Perforation increased with pre-hospital times, from 2629 (22·9%) of 11 487 patients at less than 12 h (reference) to 2671 (25·8%) of 10 371 at 12-23 h (aRR 1·07 [95% CI 1·01-1·13]; p=0·021), 2969 (33·6%) of 8826 at 24-47 h (1·36 [1·28-1·44]; p<0·0001), 1933 (41·7%) of 4640 at 48-71 h (1·62 [1·52-1·72]; p<0·0001), and 3350 (48·0%) of 6974 at pre-hospital times of at least 72 h (1·85 [1·75-1·95]; p<0·0001). Longer in-hospital time was associated with lower perforation risk: versus less than 12 h, aRRs were 0·95 (95% CI 0·91-1·00; p=0·034) for 12-23 h, 0·87 (0·82-0·93; p<0·0001) for 24-47 h, and 0·82 (0·75-0·90; p<0·0001) for at least 48 h. Perforation was associated with higher complication risk at 30 days (2·36 [2·24-2·48]; p<0·0001). Complications were also higher after open surgery than for minimally invasive surgery (1·30 [1·20-1·41]; p<0·0001). Negative appendicectomy occurred in 2365 (5·2%) of 45 218 patients and was lower among those who had preoperative CT than among those who did not (0·69 [0·62-0·77]; p<0·0001). INTERPRETATION: These findings support prioritising surgical assessment within 24 h as a target to reduce the burden of perforated appendicitis. Preoperative CT imaging was associated with lower rates of unnecessary operations; access to CT and minimally invasive surgery varied markedly by country income group. FUNDING: National Institute for Health and Care Research.

title: Diagnostic performance and testing costs of pooled testing for molecular detection of tuberculosis in seven countries: a prospective, observational, diagnostic accuracy study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Globally in 2024, only 54% of people diagnosed with tuberculosis received an initial WHO-recommended rapid molecular diagnostic test. Pooled testing could expand access to molecular detection using existing laboratory capacity. We aimed to evaluate the performance of pooled tuberculosis testing in a multicentre diagnostic accuracy study. METHODS: In this prospective diagnostic accuracy study, we enrolled individuals with presumptive tuberculosis through facility-based case finding (district hospitals and primary health centres) and community-based case finding in Bangladesh, Brazil, Cameroon, Kenya, Malawi, Nigeria, and Viet Nam between Nov 30, 2023, and Feb 27, 2025. Sputum was tested individually on Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra (Xpert Ultra) and in pools of two, three, or four specimens on Xpert Ultra. Culture was used as the microbiological reference standard. We estimated the sensitivity and specificity of pooled testing versus culture, positive percent agreement (PPA) versus individual Xpert Ultra, and cartridge savings. FINDINGS: Results were available for 14 040 (95·2%) participants from 3666 pools, including 3195 (87·2%) pools of four. Using culture as the reference standard, sensitivity of pooled testing versus individual Xpert Ultra was 84·9% (95% CI 82·5-87·0) versus 88·0% (85·9-90·0), and specificity was 98·3% (98·0-98·5) versus 97·7% (97·4-97·9). PPA was 90·1% (95% CI 88·4-91·7), remaining above 96% for high (98·1% [96·1-99·2]), medium (98·3% [95·8-99·5]), and low (96·5% [93·8-98·2]) individual Xpert Ultra semiquantitative grades, but lower for very low (86·6% [79·9-91·7]) and trace (55·4% [47·9-62·7]) grades. Pooled testing used 7028 cartridges versus 14 362 for individual testing, a 51·1% reduction. INTERPRETATION: Pooled testing with Xpert Ultra had slightly higher specificity and a 3·2 percentage points lower sensitivity compared with individual Xpert Ultra, and required half the cartridge use. Scale-up of this approach could facilitate expanded access to molecular testing in low to moderate tuberculosis positivity settings without the need for additional infrastructure. FUNDING: Unitaid.

title: Burden of schistosomiasis in Ethiopia following 10 years of preventive chemotherapy: a national cross-sectional geostatistical survey
abstract: Background Current strategies aim to eliminate schistosomiasis as a public health problem globally by 2030. As this target approaches, up-to-date knowledge of the burden and distribution of schistosomiasis is crucial. After a decade of control measures in Ethiopia, there are currently no high-resolution data with which to evaluate progress and guide interventions. Through a nationwide survey, we aimed to map the fine-scale distribution of schistosomiasis in Ethiopia to guide programmatic decision making at the kebele (subdistrict) level. Methods This cross-sectional geostatistical survey was conducted across ten regions of Ethiopia using spatially regulated sampling. Children aged 9–14 years were selected, using sex-stratified systematic random sampling, from schools or communities. Stool samples, collected from children in all ten regions, were assessed for Schistosoma mansoni using the Kato–Katz thick smear technique. Schistosoma haematobium infection was assessed by urine filtration and a urine dipstick test from samples obtained from children in three endemic regions. We fitted geostatistical models incorporating environmental covariates from five domains: sociodemographic, bioclimate, geology, land cover, and exposure to contaminated water. We generated 1 km 2 prevalence maps and estimated the probability of exceeding WHO preventive chemotherapy thresholds at the kebele level. The primary outcomes were the prevalences of infection and heavy-intensity infection with S mansoni and S haematobium . Findings Between June 20, 2021, and Oct 22, 2024, 121 593 children were enrolled at 4258 sites. Complete datasets for S mansoni analysis were available from 119 559 children surveyed at 4100 sites, among whom 26 885 were also assessed for S haematobium . The mean age of the children was 11·4 years (SD 1·7), with 57 046 (47·7%) female and 62 513 (52·3%) male. The combined survey prevalence of both Schistosoma species analysed was 5·4% (95% CI 5·0–5·9): 5·2% (4·8–5·7) for S mansoni and 1·0% (0·8–1·3) for S haematobium . Compared with baseline defined woreda-level prevalence categories, areas with a prevalence of at least 10% have declined, reducing the number of people above the threshold for requiring annual preventive chemotherapy from 25·6 million to 10·8 million. 1622 (11·0%) of 14 763 assessed kebeles were above the threshold for annual preventive chemotherapy, and the predicted probability of correct classification was at least 70% for 11 600 (78·6%) of the 14 763 kebeles. The prevalence of heavy-intensity infection among the survey population was 0·2% (95% CI 0·2 to 0·3) overall (0·2% [0·2 to 0·3] for S mansoni and <0·1% [<0·1 to <0·1] for S haematobium ), below the WHO elimination as a public health problem target of 1%. Interpretation This national, high-resolution map of schistosomiasis in Ethiopia shows marked progress towards elimination. The model-based geostatistical approach supports targeted, evidence-driven interventions and more efficient use of resources. Funding END Fund's Deworming Innovation Fund, which receives funding from anchor partners including the ELMA Foundation, Delta Philanthropies, the Children's Investment Fund Foundation, the Wyss Medical Foundation, and Virgin Unite through an Audacious Project.

title: Hookworm and Strongyloides stercoralis infections in school-age children and cohabiting dogs in Cambodia following 5 years of bi-annual mass drug administration: a cross-sectional observational study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Despite sustained control efforts, soil-transmitted helminths remain a major public health burden in endemic regions, with companion animals, particularly dogs, acting as potential reservoirs further complicating elimination efforts. In this study we aimed to assess infection levels in school-age children following 5 years of bi-annual school-based deworming and to investigate the contribution of dogs to ongoing zoonotic transmission in rural Cambodia. METHODS: A cross-sectional observational study was conducted across 14 villages and five primary schools in Ta Ches commune, Kampong Chhnang province, Cambodia. These primary schools were receiving bi-annual preventive chemotherapy and villages within the commune were chosen based on the residential locations of the children attending these schools. All children aged 6-15 years enrolled in grades 1-6 attending the five participating schools and dog owners residing in the 14 villages were invited to participate. No random sampling or stratification was applied. Human and dog faecal samples were collected and screened using quantitative PCR. Samples from either children or dogs containing insufficient faecal material for DNA extraction were excluded. DNA sequencing and robust statistical approaches were performed to investigate zoonotic transmission dynamics between children and cohabiting dogs. The primary outcome of this study was the level of soil-transmitted helminth infections. FINDINGS: Between Dec 2, and Dec 15, 2019, 706 children and 474 cohabiting dogs were included in the study. Soil-transmitted helminths were detected in 320 (45% [95% CI 42-49]) of 706 children, with hookworm infections predominating (302 [43%; 40-47]). Moderate-heavy infections exceeded the 2% WHO threshold needed for elimination. In 10 (71%; 50-93) of 14 villages, children and dogs harboured Ancylostoma ceylanicum, Strongyloides stercoralis, or a combination of the two, with combined zoonotic infections in 47 (15%; 11-19) children. We found that A ceylanicum and S stercoralis sequences from dogs and children clustered together with no clear distinction. However, the higher S stercoralis haplotype diversity in children compared with dogs suggests that S stercoralis transmission in our human population is complex, likely involving a potentially prevalent human-to-human transmission. INTERPRETATION: Despite 5 years of targeted bi-annual mass drug administration, hookworms and S stercoralis remain a major public health issue in Cambodia. Our findings highlight the limitations of school-based deworming strategies and underscore the need for integrated molecular surveillance and One Health interventions to achieve the 2030 soil-transmitted helminths elimination targets. FUNDING: The University of Melbourne McKenzie Fellowship and the Soulsby Foundation.

title: Global, regional, and national burden of exposure to chewing tobacco, 1990–2023: a systematic analysis of the Global Burden of Disease Study 2023
abstract: BACKGROUND: Exposure to chewing tobacco is a known health risk factor but has received less attention than smoking in global tobacco control efforts. As the evidence base linking chewing tobacco use to poor health grows, it is essential to closely track the changing use of chewing tobacco distinct from other forms of smokeless tobacco, as well as the estimated burden associated with its use. These data are essential to inform policy makers who seek to identify and avert the health burden associated with these dangerous products. METHODS: We estimated the prevalence of chewing tobacco use and attributable health burden for individuals aged 15 years and older across 204 countries and territories by age and sex to produce temporal estimates from 1990 to 2023 as part of the Global Burden of Diseases, Injuries, and Risk Factors Study 2023. We leveraged self-reported survey data on use of any smokeless tobacco products spanning 188 countries globally to inform estimates of chewing tobacco use. Further, we undertook a systematic review and meta-analysis using the burden of proof methodology to generate associated relative risks. Together, these estimates served as inputs to generate cause-specific, location-specific, age-specific, sex-specific, and year-specific population-attributable fractions and the resulting attributable measures of health burden. FINDINGS: In 2023, we estimate 241 million (95% uncertainty interval [UI] 165-355) users of chewing tobacco globally, a prevalence of 3·9% (95% UI 2·7-5·8) among individuals aged 15 years and older. Consumption was concentrated in south Asia, where India had 64·3% (56·1-71·8) of all male chewing tobacco users and 54·8% (47·1-62·4) of all female users. Bangladesh followed with 7·6% (6·0-9·6) and 19·0% (14·5-24·6) of all male and female chewing tobacco users, respectively. Globally, use peaked in older ages, with a prevalence of 5·1% (3·2-8·0) among people aged 60-64 years. Chewing tobacco use was linked to 251 thousand deaths (149-389) in 2023, 152 thousand (96·2-235) of which occurred in males and 99·7 thousand (53·2-164) in females. When adding years of life lost to disability, the total burden attributed to chewing tobacco use was 6·48 million (3·96-9·91) disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) in 2023. This burden corresponds to 133·5 (85·8-201·8) DALYs per 100 000 males and 66·9 (35·6-109·9) DALYs per 100 000 females. The burden attributable to chewing tobacco was linked to six outcomes, the largest of which was stroke (55·9 [29·0-92·9] DALYs per 100 000 individuals attributable to chewing tobacco) followed by lip and oral cavity cancer (17·4 [11·3-24·3] DALYs per 100 000). However, the underlying epidemiological evidence ranges from moderate to weak. INTERPRETATION: We observed little change over time in the prevalence of chewing tobacco use, accompanied by a growing burden of associated death and disability. This burden of stroke and head and neck cancers is seen most heavily in south Asia. Chewing tobacco remains an understudied risk factor of public health concern and requires signatories of the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control to increase efforts to reduce exposure alongside those made to mitigate the harms of other tobacco products. FUNDING: Bloomberg Philanthropies and Gates Foundation.

title: Chewing tobacco: the neglected component of the tobacco epidemic
abstract: In their analysis published in The Lancet Global Health, the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2023 Chewing Tobacco Collaborators highlight a persistent and neglected challenge in a global health landscape in which tobacco control has made substantial progress.1 Their comprehensive study shows that despite decades of global tobacco-control efforts, 241 million people used chewing tobacco in 2023, with use concentrated in south Asia and prevalence changing little since 1990.1 The analysis adds crucial granularity to our understanding of this risk factor, estimating 251 000 deaths and 6·48 million disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) attributable to chewing tobacco in 2023.

title: Symptom-agnostic endpoints in tuberculosis vaccine efficacy trials
abstract: Tuberculosis vaccine prevention-of-disease efficacy trials traditionally rely on symptom-triggered case detection. This approach captures only a subset of bacteriologically confirmed disease and can miss cases that occur between scheduled trial visits or outside trial procedures, slowing endpoint accrual and complicating interpretation of results. At the same time, the diagnostic landscape for tuberculosis is changing rapidly. Advances, including near point-of-care (NPOC) molecular assays using sputum and non-sputum specimens, portable chest radiography with computer-aided detection, and digital tools for decentralised monitoring, now make symptom-agnostic screening strategies increasingly feasible in large clinical trials. A 2026 WHO policy recommending the use of NPOC molecular diagnostics for tuberculosis further highlights the relevance of these approaches. In this Health Policy paper, we outlined a framework for integrating symptom-agnostic screening into tuberculosis vaccine efficacy trials and reviewed emerging diagnostic technologies that could enable this transition. Using parameters informed by the placebo arm of the M72/AS01 E phase 2b trial, we present a worked example illustrating a possible effect on endpoint detection and case-verification burden. In this illustrative scenario, an NPOC-based symptom-agnostic screening strategy was estimated to increase detection of bacteriologically confirmed tuberculosis endpoints by approximately 1·4-fold, as compared with that by symptom-based screening alone, although this finding should not be interpreted as a direct estimate of overall trial efficiency. Realising these benefits will require analytical validation of diagnostic tools, clinical qualification for trial use, and early alignment with regulators and policy bodies. If evaluated through staged evidence generation and implemented with stringent confirmation algorithms, then symptom-agnostic screening could support more interpretable assessments of vaccine impact across the bacteriological spectrum of tuberculosis disease while preserving endpoint specificity.

title: Beyond diagnostic accuracy: defining the role of tongue swabs in decentralised tuberculosis screening
abstract: In 2026, after almost a decade of research, WHO recommended tongue swabs for tuberculosis nucleic acid amplification testing in adults when sputum is unavailable, after noting decreased tongue swab sensitivity compared with sputum.1 This recommendation moved the central research question to whether tongue swab testing can meaningfully expand current tuberculosis screening strategies. Andrew Medina-Marino and colleagues, in their Article published in The Lancet Global Health, provide an important contribution to this discussion by evaluating in-home tuberculosis molecular testing.

title: The burden and long-term outcomes of diagnosed and underdiagnosed COPD across diverse communities from high-income, middle-income, and low-income countries: the Prospective Urban Rural Epidemiology (PURE) study
authors: Fatin Azierah Fauzi Siti Norzulikha Rahim
abstract: BACKGROUND: Airflow obstruction detected on spirometry is a hallmark of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and is needed for the diagnosis of COPD. Sparse data in high-income countries (HICs) have reported high prevalence of underdiagnosed COPD with poor clinical outcomes. Data are missing for low-income and middle-income countries (LMICs) to inform the burden and clinical outcomes of underdiagnosed COPD. METHODS: In this multinational, prospective cohort study, spirometry data were systematically collected from adults (aged 35-70 years) in urban and rural communities across 25 HICs and LMICs. Adults with spirometry airflow obstruction with physician-diagnosed airway diseases were categorised as diagnosed COPD and those without physician-diagnosed airway diseases were categorised as underdiagnosed COPD. Individuals with normal spirometry and no known airway diseases were categorised as no COPD. Data on baseline characteristics were collected via standardised interview questionnaires and follow-up data were collected every 3 years on vital status and clinical events. We examined the association between COPD status with baseline characteristics and follow-up clinical events. FINDINGS: Between July 11, 2002, and July 28, 2025, we collected data on 119 252 participants (baseline median age 51 years [IQR 43-59], 71 039 [59·6%] females and 48 213 (40·4%) males) with technically acceptable spirometry. The prevalence of airflow obstruction was 9·5% (11 306/119 252), of which 89·2% (10 080/11 306) constituted underdiagnosed COPD. The prevalence of airflow obstruction varied across geographical regions (6·1% [n=521/8601] in southeast Asia to 20·4% [n=785/3846] in sub-Saharan Africa) and was higher in LMICs (9·8% [n=10 120/103 758]) than in HICs (7·7% [n=1186/15 494]), with a prevalence of 90·7% (9175/10 120) for underdiagnosed COPD in LMICs. Baseline characteristics associated with underdiagnosis were younger age (≤50 years), low symptom burden, high lung function, being current or never smokers, and living in an LMIC. Compared with no COPD, underdiagnosed and diagnosed COPD were associated with higher mortality (hazard ratio 1·53 [95% CI 1·44-1·63] for underdiagnosed and 2·09 [1·83-2·40] for diagnosed COPD), respiratory events (1·97 [1·82-2·12] for underdiagnosed and 3·70 [3·25-4·21] for diagnosed COPD), and cardiovascular events (1·20 [1·13-1·27] for underdiagnosed and 1·35 [1·17-1·56] for diagnosed COPD). This association was consistent across country-income levels, age groups, smoking status, and symptom burden. INTERPRETATION: The high prevalence of underdiagnosed COPD and related poor outcomes suggest that a large burden of COPD is under-recognised. Since underdiagnosed COPD is mainly early and mild disease, this presents missed opportunities for early intervention that can modify disease trajectory and improve long-term health outcomes. FUNDING: AstraZeneca, Population Health Research Institute, Hamilton Health Sciences Research Institute, the Canadian Institutes of Health Research, Heart and Stroke Foundation of Ontario, Canadian Institutes of Health Research's Strategy for Patient Oriented Research, Ontario SPOR Support Unit, and Ontario Ministry of Health and Long-Term Care.

title: HIV service delivery after the PEPFAR and USAID HIV funding withdrawal in Uganda and Zimbabwe: an interrupted time-series study
abstract: BACKGROUND: In January 2025, the US Government froze foreign aid and halted the President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), the largest external funder of HIV services globally. Early modelling studies and rapid assessments warned of major harm to millions, but robust quantitative evidence from those who relied most on the lost funding has been absent. We aimed to estimate the effect of the US funding withdrawal on HIV prevention, pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), testing, and treatment services provided by non-governmental organisations (NGOs) serving primarily key populations in Uganda and Zimbabwe. METHODS: In this interrupted time-series study, we used monthly and quarterly service-delivery data from NGOs in Uganda and Zimbabwe from January 2023 up to March 2026. All received stop-work orders and subsequent funding cuts. Core service indicators across prevention, PrEP, treatment, and testing were normalised into domain indices, in which 100 represents their mean 2024 amount. The main outcome was the change in these service indicators because of funding cuts. Specifying February 2025 as the interruption point, we estimated effects with an unweighted panel interrupted time-series (the organisation level) and a client-weighted interrupted time-series (the key-population level) on these indices. FINDINGS: Eight organisations agreed to participate; four were subsequently excluded for reasons of data quality, lack of funding impact, and location, with four subsequently included in this study. All four service domains showed large, sustained declines. Across both the unweighted and weighted specifications, prevention fell by 36·8-62·7 index points, PrEP by 43·0-71·6, treatment by 22·0-31·5, and testing by 58·7-63·8 index points in February 2025 (index points are equivalent to percentage change from mean 2024 amounts). 95% CIs excluded zero for all estimates except PrEP in the unweighted panel. Services remained substantially below the 2024 amount up to March 2026. The antiretroviral therapy humanitarian waiver attenuated treatment effects but did not prevent substantial decline. INTERPRETATION: The sudden withdrawal of US funding was followed by severe, sustained disruptions to HIV service delivery in Uganda and Zimbabwe across all major domains, with the largest declines in prevention, PrEP, and testing services for key populations. These results are the first quantitative findings on service-volume changes in NGOs whose US funding was terminated or sharply cut and illustrate the effect on the NGO-led, key-population layer of HIV services in sub-Saharan Africa. These services are crucial to people living with HIV to remain healthy and have a good quality of life. Urgent investment in service-continuity protocols and domestic financing is needed to prevent a rebound in HIV incidence. FUNDING: The Josiah Charles Trent Memorial Foundation Endowment Fund, the Sanford School of Public Policy, and Duke Global Publications Fund.

title: Large reductions in HIV services for key populations in sub-Saharan Africa
abstract: In this issue of The Lancet Global Health, Henry Cust, Sungai T Chabata, and other unnamed collaborators1 report one of the first quantitative, real-world studies of abrupt and sustained cessation of the US Government funding for HIV services, primarily delivered to populations at highest risk of HIV acquisition—key populations—by four non-governmental organisations in Uganda and Zimbabwe. The interrupted time-series study used monthly and quarterly service-delivery data from the non-governmental organisations in the two countries from January, 2023 to March, 2026 to estimate the effects of the stop-work orders they received and subsequent funding cuts.

title: Hospital-based prevalence of culture-confirmed melioidosis among high-risk patients in India, 2023–25: a multicentre prospective study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Melioidosis is not a nationally notifiable disease in India, and the absence of systematic surveillance has contributed to substantial under-recognition and fragmented epidemiological data. We aimed to determine the hospital-based prevalence of culture-confirmed melioidosis among hospitalised adults at high risk of melioidosis in India. METHODS: We conducted a prospective, multicentre, hospital-based prevalence study between Jan 1, 2023, and Dec 31, 2025, across 15 tertiary care centres in India. Adults (aged ≥18 years) hospitalised with predefined community-acquired infectious syndromes and diabetes or chronic kidney disease were enrolled. Melioidosis was defined by culture confirmation. The primary outcome was hospital-based prevalence. Prespecified secondary analyses assessed geographical, syndrome-specific, and seasonal variation; factors associated with melioidosis; and clinical characteristics and in-hospital outcomes. FINDINGS: Among 2953 patients, 262 (8·9% [95% CI 7·9-10·0]) had culture-confirmed melioidosis, with marked geographical heterogeneity. Prevalence was highest in Odisha, Madhya Pradesh, and Karnataka, and among patients presenting with extrapulmonary abscesses and bone and joint infections. Cases clustered during the monsoon months. Factors independently associated with melioidosis included monsoon admission (adjusted odds ratio 1·40 [95% CI 1·08-1·83]), male sex (2·33 [1·64-3·32]), outdoor high-risk occupation (1·94 [1·47-2·56]), and groundwater as the primary drinking-water source (3·25 [2·48-4·26]). Bacteraemia occurred in 152 (58%) of 262 patients with melioidosis, and 50 (19%) died in hospital. INTERPRETATION: Melioidosis is a frequent and severe infection among high-risk hospitalised adults in India, with substantial geographical variation and strong environmental and seasonal associations. These findings support targeted diagnostic testing and heightened clinical awareness among high-risk patients. FUNDING: Indian Council of Medical Research.

title: Expression of concern—Effect of Brazil’s national human papillomavirus vaccination programme on the incidence of cervical cancer and cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 3 in women aged 20–24 years: a population-based study
authors: The Editors of The Lancet Global Health
abstract: In October 2025, The Lancet Global Health published a population-based study to estimate the effect of Brazil’s national human papillomavirus vaccination programme on the incidence of cervical cancer,1 by Thiago Cerqueira-Silva and colleagues. On July 15, 2026, the corresponding author alerted us to some coding errors that affected several numerical values in the findings—some substantially. In view of the extent of these errors, we now issue an Expression of Concern while working with the authors to correct the record, including further review of the revised paper.

title: Mortality and disability after hospitalisation for injuries in low-income and middle-income countries: a cohort study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Mortality and disability after injuries are high in low-income and middle-income countries (LMICs). Improving outcomes for injured patients requires knowledge of their associated factors. We aimed to assess post-injury mortality and disability and their associations with access to health care across LMICs with different injury burdens, health-care systems, and contexts. METHODS: Hospitalised patients in Ghana, Pakistan, Rwanda, and South Africa with moderate-to-severe injuries were recruited and followed up until 3 months after discharge or death. Injured patients of any age who were admitted to facilities for more than 12 h or died within 12 h of admission were included. Data were collected between Feb 17, 2023, and Aug 31, 2024, using the REDCap electronic data platform. Our primary outcome was a composite of 3-month mortality or moderate-to-severe disability (assessed using the WHO Disability Assessment Schedule). Secondary outcomes were disability at 3 months after discharge, mortality up to 3 months after discharge (including in-hospital mortality), and in-hospital mortality. In multivariable analysis, we tested the associations of these outcomes with access to health-care variables of previous health-care encounters, transport to the hospital (private vs ambulance vs other), delays in reaching the hospital, and hospital level (secondary vs tertiary), controlling for age, sex, education, wealth, and injury type and severity. FINDINGS: 9720 patients admitted to 19 hospitals capable of providing definitive care for injuries, serving urban and rural settings, were eligible for inclusion in the study. Of those, 8858 (91·1%; 6788 male, 2047 female, and 23 [<1%] with missing sex data; median age 31 years [IQR 20-43]) were enrolled and 8687 (89·4%) completed hospital follow-up, with 5835 patients followed up at 3 months. At 3 months, 2476 (47·6%) of 5199 patients with available primary outcome data had died or were disabled. In-hospital mortality was 6·1% (531 of 8687), 3-month mortality was 9·7% (616 of 6366), and 3-month disability was 40·6% (1860 of 4583). Higher odds of the primary outcome were associated with arrival by ambulance (odds ratio 1·86, 95% CI 1·51-2·29), and lower odds were associated with a previous health-care encounter (0·61, 0·52-0·71). Hospital level (1·14, 0·96-1·35) and delays in reaching the facility (0·86, 0·74-1·00) were not associated with the primary outcome. INTERPRETATION: The high post-injury mortality and disability are associated with health system factors that must be better understood before potentially expensive service models are introduced or expanded. Investment in pre-hospital care, ambulance systems, and centralised specialist trauma centres is unlikely to achieve its intended benefits unless services are appropriately planned, integrated, coordinated, and staffed across the care pathway. High-quality routine data are also essential to guide service improvement and enable robust quasi-experimental evaluations of whether these investments improve patient outcomes, for whom, and under what circumstances. FUNDING: National Institute for Health and Care Research.

title: Informing an mpox stockpile investment case: epidemiological modelling and cost–benefit analysis
abstract: BACKGROUND: In response to ongoing mpox outbreaks, Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, was considering funding the establishment of an mpox vaccine stockpile. To support their decision making, Gavi commissioned the Center for Outbreak Response Innovation at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health to estimate the optimal size, impact, health benefits, and monetised net benefits of different mpox vaccine stockpile sizes for an effective global stockpile to support outbreak containment and prevention of widespread mpox transmission. We aimed to quantify the potential impact of vaccination on future mpox outbreaks to inform Gavi's decision making for investing in an effective mpox vaccine stockpile. METHODS: A deterministic compartmental model of mpox transmission with vaccine interventions was developed, including intervening rapidly-at 20 cases reported-versus at 100 cases reported. The model was used to assess potential vaccine-based mitigation strategies for mpox outbreaks in Gavi-eligible countries by simulating mpox transmission and control dynamics, given two vaccination strategies (one dose and two doses) compared with no intervention in high-risk groups and contacts of cases, across four distinct subpopulations: (1) children younger than 5 years, (2) men who have sex with men, (3) female sex workers, and (4) the remaining general population. The findings from this model were incorporated into a Monte Carlo cost-benefit analysis of different stockpile sizes. FINDINGS: Rapid response (ie, intervening at 20 cases reported) using a single-dose vaccination strategy provided the greatest benefits relative to costs compared with a two-dose strategy. Using a one-dose strategy, expected net benefits were estimated to be over US$81 million to $220 million higher when responding to outbreaks rapidly than when responding after 100 cases. Furthermore, the total cost per disability-adjusted life-year (DALY) averted with rapid response using a one-dose vaccine strategy responding at 20 cases was 18% to 53% lower than a one-dose strategy introduced at 100 cases. A stockpile of 1 000 000 doses had the highest ratio of benefits to costs. INTERPRETATION: A stockpile calibrated to attain a high ratio of benefits to costs can be effective in controlling outbreaks and reducing overall negative health impacts. The cost-effectiveness of mpox vaccine stockpiles could be further maximised with reduced vaccine pricing and dose-sparing strategies. FUNDING: Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance.

title: Children with arthritis: orphans of the NCD agenda?
abstract: Musculoskeletal conditions, including forms of inflammatory arthritis such as juvenile idiopathic arthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, and axial spondyloarthritis, are leading causes of disability-adjusted life-years globally. In 2020, 17·6 million people were estimated to have rheumatoid arthritis, and juvenile idiopathic arthritis affected more than 2 million children worldwide. These conditions present a substantial threat to healthy ageing, causing chronic pain, limiting mobility and reducing participation in education and employment.

title: Interpreting the lifetime risk of maternal near miss
abstract: Maternal near miss (MNM) events, during pregnancy, childbirth, and the postpartum period, are life-threatening complications in which a woman almost dies but survives.1 WHO identifies MNM cases based on clinical, laboratory, and management-based indicators of organ dysfunction.1 Quantifying the burden of these events across the reproductive life course can reveal how inequities in maternal outcomes accumulate through differences in obstetric risk per pregnancy and repeated exposure across successive pregnancies.

title: Artificial intelligence-supported diabetic retinopathy screening in Tanzania: a randomised controlled trial
abstract: BACKGROUND: Non-attendance after referral from screening is one of the major challenges for diabetic retinopathy screening programmes in Africa. Artificial intelligence (AI) systems for the identification of diabetic retinopathy can provide point-of-screening results and therefore enable immediate counselling. We aimed to investigate whether AI-supported diabetic retinopathy screening, with a point-of-screening result and face-to-face counselling, increased the proportion of people with true referable diabetic retinopathy who attended the central ophthalmology referral clinic when compared with standard diabetic retinopathy screening with deferred human grading and telephone counselling. METHODS: This two-arm, parallel-group, individually randomised controlled trial was conducted at non-communicable disease or diabetic clinics in 24 hospitals in the Kilimanjaro and Arusha regions of Tanzania. Eligible participants (aged ≥18 years) had diabetes and attended diabetic retinopathy screening. Participants were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive either AI-supported diabetic retinopathy screening with a point-of-screening result and face-to-face counselling (the AI-intervention group) or standard-of-care diabetic retinopathy screening with deferred human retinal image assessment and telephone counselling (the standard-of-care group). Participants had retinal photographs taken of both eyes. Images from the AI-intervention group were submitted to the AI software, and these participants were given their screening result (non-referable, referable, or ungradable) plus face-to-face counselling before leaving the photography room, with a referral to the central ophthalmology clinic if the AI output was referable or ungradable. Participants in the standard-of-care group received their screening result, along with appropriate counselling, by telephone a few weeks later. The primary outcome was attendance at the central ophthalmology clinic within 8 weeks of screening among participants classified by masked UK-certified graders as having true referable diabetic retinopathy. This trial was registered with the ISRCTN Registry, ISRCTN18317152, and is complete. FINDINGS: Between March 8, 2023, and Aug 31, 2024, 2439 participants were assessed for eligibility and 2378 were enrolled, of whom 1192 were randomly assigned to the AI-intervention group and 1186 to the standard-of-care group. 904 participants had true referable diabetic retinopathy, comprising 437 in the AI-intervention group and 467 in the standard-of-care group. Of the participants in the AI-intervention group, 157 (35·9%) of 437 attended the central ophthalmology clinic within 8 weeks, compared with 85 (18·2%) of 467 in the standard-of-care group, an absolute difference of 17·7 percentage points (95% CI 12·0-23·4; odds ratio 2·52 [95% CI 1·86-3·42]; p<0·0001). INTERPRETATION: AI-supported screening, with a point-of-screening result and face-to-face counselling, increased the proportion of people with true referable diabetic retinopathy that attended the central ophthalmology clinic after screening compared with the standard of care in Tanzania. Such AI-enabled screening pathways have the potential to improve diabetic retinopathy screening programmes in Africa. FUNDING: British Council for the Prevention of Blindness, Christian Blind Mission, and the Sir Halley Stewart Trust.

title: Refining global models for large-scale food fortification
abstract: We read with great interest the modelling analysis by Valerie M Friesen and colleagues, published in the Lancet Global Health, that provides a comprehensive global assessment of large-scale food fortification and its cost-effectiveness across diverse settings.1 The integration of dietary intake distributions with fortification programme parameters is an important step towards quantifying population-level nutritional gains.

title: Refining global models for large-scale food fortification
2022 WHO estimates for overall and human papillomavirus test-based cervical cancer screening coverage worldwide: a review and synthetic analysis
abstract: BACKGROUND: Regularly updated global estimates are needed to monitor progress in cervical cancer screening, a key pillar of WHO's strategy to eliminate cervical cancer. We aimed to update estimates of cervical cancer screening coverage in 194 WHO member states and eight associated countries and territories for 2022, including the first global assessment of human papillomavirus (HPV) test-based screening adoption and roll-out. METHODS: In this review and synthetic analysis, we used an established method to estimate standardised cervical cancer screening coverage in 2022. We used programme and population-based coverage data collected up to Jan 31, 2024, selecting the sources considered most representative of each country or territory's screening situation in 2022. Preliminary estimates were reviewed through a WHO country consultation (April-May, 2024; with additional responses received until July 2025). HPV testing coverage was estimated based on HPV test-based screening implementation levels, by country and year. Estimates were applied to 2022 populations and aggregated by region and country-income level. FINDINGS: Cervical cancer screening recommendations were identified in 161 (80%) of 202 countries, with 92 (57%) of 161 countries recommending HPV test-based screening. By 2022, global coverage for women aged 30-49 years using any screening method (ie, cytology, HPV test, visual inspection with acetic acid, or combinations of these methods) was estimated at 19% (95% CI 15-22) for the previous year, 31% (26-35) in the previous 3 years, and 35% (30-39) in the previous 5 years; and 38% (33-43) of women had ever been screened. Disparities across regions and country-income levels were substantial: 5-year coverage was 26% (21-31) in low-income and middle-income countries, compared with 74% (64-84) in high-income countries. 5-year HPV test-based screening coverage was 8% (6-9) globally, 32% (25-40) in high-income countries, and 2% (2-3) in low-income and middle-income countries. In the past 5 years, 62 countries achieved more than 70% coverage with any screening method, and five countries with HPV testing. INTERPRETATION: Despite policy updates, overall and HPV-specific screening coverage remains far below WHO's 70% target. Three in five women aged 30-49 years worldwide have never been screened, and 92% have never received HPV testing, with substantial disparities across regions and country-income levels. Scaling up high-performance HPV test-based screening, alongside HPV vaccination, will be essential to accelerate cervical cancer elimination. FUNDING: WHO, Instituto de Salud Carlos III, European Regional Development Fund, Secretariat for Universities and Research, Government of Catalonia, and Horizon 2020.

title: Expression of concern: Global feasibility of cervical cancer elimination: a multidimensional scenario-based modelling analysis across 175 countries
abstract: On July 2, 2026, The Lancet Global Health published a multidimensional scenario-based modelling analysis to evaluate feasibility of cervical cancer elimination globally, by Mauricio A Cuello and colleagues.1 We received inquiries on Aug 2 and 9, 2026 regarding potential errors with the projection model. We have discussed these concerns with the authors, who confirmed that a replacement model is needed. In view of the extent of these errors, we now issue an Expression of Concern while working with the authors on how best to correct the record, including further review of the replacement model.

title: Accountability for pandemic financing decisions
abstract: Nelson Evaborhene and colleagues call for regionally led accountability for pandemic preparedness and highlight gaps between financial pledges and disbursement.1 I suggest that existing country-led health-sector reviews also identify financing obstacles and seek public, time-bound responses from institutions with authority to act, including funders and intermediaries whose decisions lie beyond recipient countries’ control.

title: Global health deserves better criticism
abstract: Equity has been a central principle to global health since the field emerged approximately 25–30 years ago. More recently, attention has turned inwards, towards disparities and questions of inequities within global health as a discipline. Unequal access to funding, visa and language barriers, authorship practices, and the concentration of resources and influence shape who participates in global health. Yet, observed disparities and inequities are not the same thing. A disparity is a starting point for an investigation: understanding whether it reflects inequity, what produced it, and what might change it requires explanation.

title: Prevalence of neural tube defects and major external structural abnormalities by antiretroviral treatment regimen in Botswana in 2014–22: a birth outcomes surveillance study
abstract: BACKGROUND: The Tsepamo Study reported a preliminary safety signal associating neural tube defects with dolutegravir exposure from conception in 2018, with an attenuation of this signal from 2019 onwards. We now report complete surveillance data up to August, 2022. METHODS: Tsepamo is an ongoing large birth outcomes surveillance study in public hospitals in Botswana, covering more than two-thirds of births in the country. During routine care, all live infants and stillbirths had a surface examination. Study staff recorded descriptions of abnormal exams and exposures to maternal HIV and antiretroviral drugs and took photographs of abnormalities (upon receiving maternal consent). Photographs of major abnormalities were reviewed and classified by a medical geneticist. Neural tube defects included meningocele, myelomeningocele, anencephaly, encephalocele, and iniencephaly. Abnormalities were classified as major if there was medical, surgical, or cosmetic significance. Primary analyses evaluated the prevalence of neural tube defects and major abnormalities and the age-adjusted prevalence differences between deliveries with exposure to dolutegravir at conception and those with exposure to non-dolutegravir ART at conception, with 95% CIs calculated using log binomial regression. FINDINGS: From Aug 15, 2014, to Aug 15, 2022, there were 235 727 deliveries; 235 286 (99·8%) had an evaluable infant surface exam, including 11 110 with exposure to dolutegravir at conception and 24 368 with exposure to non-dolutegravir ART at conception. Median maternal age was 31 years (IQR 26-36) for mothers with exposure to dolutegravir at conception and 33 years (29-37) for those with exposure to non-dolutegravir ART at conception. Among 235 279 deliveries for which neural tube defect status could be determined, there were 162 neural tube defects (overall prevalence 0·07%, 95% CI 0·06-0·08) and 1455 major external structural abnormalities (0·62%, 0·59-0·65). Among 11 110 exposures to dolutegravir at conception, there were 12 neural tube defects overall (0·11%, 95% CI 0·06 to 0·19), similar to non-dolutegravir ART exposure at conception (prevalence 0·10%, 0·07-0·15; 25 of 24 368; age-adjusted prevalence difference -0·02%, 95% CI -0·09 to 0·05). Prevalence of neural tube defects was higher when conception occurred in the early dry period (May-July) than the late dry period (August-October). The prevalence of neural tube defects with dolutegravir exposure at conception (0·40%) among deliveries with conception in the first year after the dolutegravir roll-out (2017) was higher than deliveries with conception in subsequent years (range 0·06-0·10). Among 235 255 deliveries, there were overall 1455 major external structural abnormalities (0·62%, 0·59-0·65). The prevalence of major external structural abnormalities was similar between deliveries with dolutegravir exposure at conception (0·75%, 95% CI 0·60 to 0·95) and those with exposures to non-dolutegravir ART at conception (0·76%, 0·66 to 0·88; age-adjusted prevalence difference -0·01%, 95% CI -0·26 to 0·11). INTERPRETATION: No detectable increase in neural tube defects or major external structural abnormalities was noted among more than 11 000 exposures to dolutegravir at conception captured in the Tsepamo Study from 2014 to 2022. These definitive data should provide reassurance to health-care providers, patients, and policy makers about the safety of dolutegravir in pregnancy. FUNDING: National Institutes of Health/Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development.

title: Tsepamo 8 years on: women’s health remains an afterthought
abstract: In May, 2018, four cases of neural tube defects among 426 infants exposed to dolutegravir at conception in the Tsepamo study in Botswana1 triggered an international scramble across WHO, the US President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), guideline committees, and health ministries that exposed the hollowness of supposed rights-based HIV programming. The European Medicines Agency and US Food and Drug Administration issued contraception-linked warnings within days. WHO’s May 2018 guidance recommended efavirenz for women of childbearing potential in the absence of reliable contraception despite dolutegravir offering better tolerability, a higher barrier to resistance, and simpler, lower-cost implementation.

title: Is global health dead?
abstract: Global health is undergoing an existential crisis. 5 years ago, we invited readers to tell us what was wrong with it, and the result was a rich catalogue of thought pieces on “The future of global health research, publishing, and practice”. Those in the field acknowledged its colonial roots and the power imbalances that remain, discussed whose knowledge and priorities count, and made proposals for change. The past 2 years, however, have seen a more grave introspection. As development assistance and donor funding have dwindled, the promise of sovereign futures and a long-overdue acceptance that “aid” and “international research partnerships” were as much about self-interest as altruism have taken a firm hold.

title: National, regional, and global trends in adolescent physical activity from 2010 to 2025: a pooled analysis of 389 surveys with 3·2 million participants from 140 countries
abstract: BACKGROUND: Physical activity during adolescence improves current and future physical and mental health and contributes to preventing non-communicable diseases. We aimed to update national, regional, and global estimates of adolescent physical activity, examine the distribution of activity across days of the week, assess trends from 2010 to 2025, and progress towards the 2030 global target. METHODS: We pooled data from population-based surveys of self-reported number of active days (≥60 min of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity) in the past week among adolescents aged 11-17 years collected in or after 2008. Using Bayesian ordinal models, we estimated the distribution of active days per week and mean active days per week, by sex, age, country, and year. Separate models were fitted for boys and girls. We computed the posterior probability that boys' statistics were higher than girls', and that mean active days per week were higher in 2025 than in 2010. We generated projections to 2030 to assess progress towards the global target of a 15% relative reduction in the percentage of adolescents reporting fewer than 7 active days per week. FINDINGS: In 2025, 24·9% (95% uncertainty interval [UI] 21·8-28·5) of adolescents globally reported 0 active days per week, and 13·9% (12·6-15·6) reported being active on 7 days per week. The global mean was 2·7 (95% UI 2·6-2·9) active days per week. Globally, there was no change detected between 2010 and 2025. No country is on track to meet the 2030 global target. Girls' mean active days per week were lower than boys' globally (2·4 [2·2-2·7] vs 3·0 [2·8-3·2], posterior probability >0·99) and in all regions (posterior probability was 0·63 in Oceania and ≥0·89 in all other regions). In central and eastern Europe and central Asia, east Asia and the Pacific, and high-income western (comprising western Europe, northern America, Australia, and New Zealand) regions, mean active days per week (3·8-4·1 vs 2·2-2·7 in other regions) and the change in mean active days per week from 2010 to 2025 (small increases of 0·1-0·3 active days vs no change detected) were more favourable than in other regions. However, in these three regions, mean active days per week declined with age (1·2-1·4 and 0·5-0·8 fewer days at age 17 years than at age 11 years for girls and boys, respectively). INTERPRETATION: Globally, adolescent physical activity remains low, especially among girls. Increasing physical activity will require effectively implemented, context-specific actions that prioritise the least active adolescents together with whole-population approaches that address socioeconomic, environmental, and cultural barriers. FUNDING: WHO Foundation, European Commission, and the Ministry of Public Health, Qatar.
